newsitem.title: UK: Benign inflation to boost US and UK government bonds.
newsitem.headline: Benign inflation to boost US and UK government bonds.

text.p: Inflation has been such a tiny blip on bond market radar screens for so long that more good news is likely to be accepted with barely a raised eyebrow.
But more good news there is.
Since the beginning of the year, the dollar has strengthened and oil prices have crumbled and analysts said on Monday U.S., British and Canadian government bonds have the most to gain.
"If you look at European bonds, the potential for further good news on inflation is limited," said John McNeill, bond market strategist at I.D.E.A. in London.
"People don't see any threat of inflation for the likes of Germany and France. Where I think there is major opportunity for a reassessment of inflation is in U.S. Treasuries," he said.
Europe and Japan are still struggling to bounce back from a downturn that has gripped them through much of the 1990s so inflation is of little concern there, analysts said.

Even a stronger dollar, which has depressed European currencies and the yen -- giving exports a boost -- is unlikely to be much of an inflationary force in countries with such large output gaps, analysts said.

"We think Germany could sustain a couple of years of growth of 3.0 to 3-1/2 percent without any real upward pressure on inflation," said Robin Marshall, chief economist at Chase in London. He adds soaring unemployment will also dampen inflation.
But inflation prospects are already well priced into continental European markets, reflected by yields of German and French bonds trading well below those of the U.S.
The good news, including a near 10 percent fall in oil prices in the last two weeks, has not been fully reflected in Treasuries, gilts and Canadian government bonds, analysts said.
"In terms of inflation, the one that offers the most potential for gains has got to be the U.S.," Adam Chester, bond strategist at Yamaichi International Europe in London.
Despite a burgeoning economy and a run up in oil prices towards the end of last year, both producer and wage inflation remained under wraps in the U.S., analysts said.

Chester said structural changes in the U.S. economy will continue to keep inflation in check. International competition will keep domestic prices restrained while weakening labour unions, productivity gains from technology and the shift to part-time and contract work will continue to rein in wages.
The economy is also expected to cool, he said.
Bond markets have not quite believed the story and the yield on the benchmark long bond rose to around 7.0 percent at the end of January from 6.5 percent at the beginning of December.
Yields have since drifted down again with U.S. January producer prices on Friday giving a further boost. Producer prices fell 0.3 percent, the first drop since October 1994.
Chester expects the downward trend to continue, noting the government's new 10-year index-linded bond currently yields around 3.2 percent.
"A 10-year even at 6.5 percent is still implying inflation of 3.4 percent longer term and that looks unduly pessimistic," he said. Ten-year U.S. bonds now yield around 6.3 percent.
Chester also favours Canadian bonds this year.

"We have seen a remarkable performance in Canadian inflation and we expect that to continue at sub-two percent for the next year or two," he said. "Thereafter the closing of the output gap in Canada should put upward pressure on inflation longer term."
Marshall at Chase, favours gilts, with sterling helping to contain inflation already at 30-year lows. "The risk is the market is too pessimistic on inflation," Marshall said.
An interest rate rise after parliamentary elections which must be held by May 22, will further help, he said.

"If you raise rates now you would put a rocket under sterling," he said. "That's off the agenda for the Conservatives but Labour I think will do it, and you've got to say inflation looks underpinned for the rest of the year."
